The retrieved documents offer different complementary details: some specify a century (14th, 16th) while others describe the long replacement process from the 7th century onward, which together illustrate the gradual transition without contradiction.

Documents d1 and d2 state Arabic overtook Coptic in the fourteenth century CE [d1,d2]. d4 says replacement followed the Arab conquest in the 7th century. d5 describes a process starting in the late 9th century, taking a few generations, with Arabic becoming the main spoken language by the early 9th century among Christians, and Coptic dying out as a spoken language by the end of the twelfth century. d8 mentions the sixteenth century. d10 says Arabic began to overtake Coptic in the 7th century and by the 15th century Coptic ceased to be a spoken language. d3 and d6 provide background on the conquest and replacement over centuries. These snippets complement each by giving different timeframes or aspects of the gradual shift.

The evidence collectively indicates Arabic overtaking Coptic was a prolonged process. While d1 and d2 pinpoint the fourteenth century as when Arabic became the most used language in Egypt, other documents describe earlier beginnings (7th century conquest) and later endpoints (15th/16th centuries for cessation of spoken Coptic). This complementary information allows answering the query by noting the transition occurred over several centuries, with a key milestone in the fourteenth century.

According to the retrieved evidence, Arabic overtook Coptic as the language most used in Egypt during the fourteenth century CE [d1][d2]. This followed the Arab conquest of Egypt in the 7th century, which initiated the process [d4][d10]. The transition was gradual, with Arabic replacing Coptic as the primary spoken language over the centuries, completing by around the fifteenth or sixteenth century when Coptic ceased to be a spoken language [d5][d8][d10].
